consensus_summary: The blind consensus overwhelmingly identifies the great fish of Jonah 1:17 as a Christological type: Jonah's three days in the fish prefigure Christ's burial and resurrection (the 'sign of Jonah,' Matt 12:39-41), with the fish simultaneously serving as God's providential instrument of judgment and rescue, and the belly figuring Sheol/the grave. Listed alternatives include the chaos-monster (Leviathan/Rahab) motif, the swallowing hostile empire (Babylon/Pharaoh) reading (marked minority), a baptismal reading, and a genre-based 'no fixed symbol' view.
book_summary: The book identifies the great fish/sea-monster as a great ruler among the 'sea of peoples' — the personal head who stands for the kingdom and state acting through him (Pharaoh for Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar for Babylon, Caesar for Rome). The ruler 'swallows' through the body politic he heads and is forced to disgorge what he swallowed. The book relegates the tomb-typology/rescue-instrument reading to a 'commonly taught' note, signaling it does not adopt it as the symbol's meaning.
consensus_core_identification: God's appointed instrument of judgment and deliverance whose swallowing of Jonah typifies Christ's three days in the tomb (death, burial, resurrection).
book_core_identification: A hostile human ruler personifying his empire/state, who devours (swallows) peoples and is compelled by God to give them back.
boundary_disagreement: The consensus centers the term on Jonah's fish as a divine rescue vehicle; the book re-centers it on imperial rulers (Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar, Caesar) as devourers. Cases the consensus treats as a minority side-reading (Jer 51:34-44 swallowing-empire imagery) become the book's core, while the consensus's central case — the fish as God's appointed instrument prefiguring the tomb — is reclassified as merely the 'common view' rather than the symbol's meaning.
material_contradiction: The consensus core makes the fish God's benevolent providential instrument whose belly typifies Christ's tomb; the book makes it a hostile devouring ruler/kingdom forced to disgorge its prey. The same referent cannot primarily be both God's rescue vehicle typifying Christ's burial and a predatory imperial power under divine judgment — the book explicitly sets the tomb-typology aside as the 'commonly taught' view it is departing from.
rationale: Although the book's identification corresponds to an alternative the consensus lists (the swallowing-empire/Babylon reading, flagged as minority in Responses A, B, and C), the classification compares core identifications. The book replaces the consensus's central referent — the providential rescue-fish typifying Christ's three days in the tomb — with a materially different one: the ruler-as-devouring-monster. Its own common-view note confirms it is consciously displacing the standard reading rather than refining its boundary. This is replacement of the central identification, not adjustment of extension within the same category, so DIVERGENT rather than REFINED. It is not NOVEL because the empire/ruler reading is recognized in the consensus alternatives.
strongest_objection: The book's reading is explicitly present in the consensus as a recognized minority alternative (Jer 51:34-44; Ezek 29:3; 32:2), so one could argue the book merely promotes a listed alternative to primary — a boundary/priority shift within the known interpretive space, arguably REFINED rather than DIVERGENT. Additionally, the printed citations (Pharaoh as the great dragon/whale, Nebuchadnezzar swallowing and being made to disgorge, Daniel's beasts as kings/kingdoms) directly and strongly attest the ruler-as-sea-monster identification, lending the book real textual footing even if the Caesar/John 19 link is more inferential.
